title: Court Halts Trump's Memorial Arch as White House Launches Promotional Website
tagline: A federal judge has paused construction of the planned 250-foot arch near Arlington National Cemetery for 14 days, while the White House promotes the project online.

image.alt: Illustration of a gold-and-granite triumphal arch behind a construction barrier, with a judge's gavel in the foreground.
image.caption: Illustration: a court order has paused construction of the planned arch.

imageCaption: A federal court has temporarily halted work on the planned Military Triumphal Arch in Washington, D.C.
bodyHtml:
Washington, D.C. — A federal court has temporarily blocked President Donald Trump from breaking ground on a planned memorial arch, but the administration is still promoting the project. The White House launched a dedicated website for the arch, which it now calls the “Military Triumphal Arch.”

U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan issued a temporary restraining order that bars construction for 14 days. The order came shortly after a federal planning commission voted to approve the project. Critics say that commission is largely made up of Trump allies.

The structure would stand about 250 feet (76 meters) tall between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery, with gold ornamentation and gray granite. Plans include an event space reached by elevators and stairs. The website does not say what the arch would cost or how it would be paid for, although some estimates run as high as $100 million.

Opponents have raised concerns about building-height limits, environmental and historic-preservation rules, and the location next to Arlington National Cemetery. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has described the arch as a monument that also has military uses, and the judge acknowledged the government’s national-security interest.

Democrats are due to take control of Congress in January, and the administration’s building projects are expected to face closer scrutiny. The restraining order is temporary, and further court action is expected.

Source

Reporting based on coverage by The Associated Press (Will Weissert), published Nov. 6, 2026. Read the original AP report.
